events.title: Bush wins the primary
events.text: George W. Bush beat John McCain in South Carolina's Republican presidential primary on 19 February.

events.title: Brown takes the seat
events.text: Henry Brown, a Republican, began ten years as the 1st District's congressman.

events.title: Ravenel Bridge opens
events.text: The Arthur Ravenel Jr. Bridge opened across the Cooper River, linking Charleston and Mount Pleasant.

events.title: Gullah Geechee corridor
events.text: Congress designated the Gullah Geechee Cultural Heritage Corridor along the coast on 12 October.

events.title: A nine-point state
events.text: John McCain carried South Carolina by nine points, its narrowest Republican margin of the period.

events.title: Boeing comes to Charleston
events.text: Boeing chose North Charleston for a 787 Dreamliner final assembly line.

events.title: Tim Scott elected
events.text: Tim Scott won the open 1st District seat with 65.4 percent.

events.title: Scott to the Senate
events.text: Tim Scott was appointed to the U.S. Senate in January, opening the House seat.

events.title: Sanford returns
events.text: On 7 May former governor Mark Sanford beat Elizabeth Colbert Busch, 54 to 45 percent, in a special election.

events.title: Mother Emanuel
events.text: On 17 June a white supremacist murdered nine worshippers at Emanuel AME Church in Charleston.

events.title: The flag comes down
events.text: On 10 July the Confederate flag was removed from the State House grounds.

events.title: Sanford re-elected
events.text: Sanford won a third full term with 58.6 percent; Donald Trump carried the state by 14 points.

events.title: Drilling plan opposed
events.text: Governor McMaster asked for South Carolina to be exempted from the federal offshore drilling plan.

events.title: Arrington beats Sanford
events.text: On 12 June Katie Arrington beat Sanford in the primary, 50.6 to 46.5 percent, hours after President Trump endorsed her.

events.title: Cunningham wins
events.text: On 6 November Joe Cunningham won by 3,982 votes, the first Democrat to win the seat since 1978.

events.title: Drilling ban passes House
events.text: In September the U.S. House passed Cunningham's bill to ban offshore drilling, 238 to 189.

events.title: Moratorium extended
events.text: In September President Trump extended the offshore drilling moratorium to South Carolina's coast.

events.title: Mace wins it back
events.text: On 3 November Nancy Mace beat Cunningham by 5,415 votes.

events.title: A new map
events.text: Governor McMaster signed a congressional map in January that redrew the 1st District.

events.title: Mace beats Arrington
events.text: On 14 June Mace beat the Trump-endorsed Arrington in the Republican primary, 53 to 45 percent.

events.title: Mace re-elected
events.text: Mace beat Annie Andrews, a pediatrician, 56.4 to 42.5 percent on the new lines.

events.title: Racial gerrymander ruling
events.text: On 6 January a three-judge federal court ruled that District 1 was a racial gerrymander.

events.title: African American museum
events.text: The International African American Museum opened at Gadsden's Wharf on 27 June.

events.title: Supreme Court reverses
events.text: On 23 May, in Alexander v. South Carolina NAACP, the Supreme Court upheld the map, 6 to 3.

events.title: Mace's third term
events.text: Mace beat Michael B. Moore, a descendant of Robert Smalls, 58.2 to 41.6 percent.

events.title: Fastest-growing state
events.text: South Carolina grew 1.5 percent from 2024 to 2025, the fastest of any state.

events.title: Mace runs for governor
events.text: On 4 August Nancy Mace launched a campaign for governor at The Citadel, leaving the House seat open.

events.title: Lacore removed
events.text: On 22 August Defense Secretary Hegseth removed Vice Admiral Nancy Lacore as Chief of Navy Reserve.

events.title: Honeycutt enters
events.text: On 17 November Charleston County Councilwoman Jenny Costa Honeycutt announced her campaign.

events.title: Lacore enters
events.text: On 20 January Lacore, by then living in Mount Pleasant, entered the Democratic primary.

events.title: Libertarian nominee
events.text: On 13 April the Libertarian convention nominated Bill Reeside, a retired nuclear engineer from Edisto Beach.

events.title: Sanford withdraws
events.text: On 29 April Mark Sanford ended his comeback bid; his name stayed on the primary ballot.

events.title: Redraw stalls
events.text: On 26 May the state Senate shelved a new congressional map, 26 to 18; 2026 is fought on the 2022 lines.

events.title: Hilton Head debate
events.text: On 28 May five Republican candidates debated on Hilton Head Island.

events.title: Primary day
events.text: On 9 June Honeycutt led the Republican primary with 22.1 percent; Lacore led the Democratic one with 36.5.

events.title: Mace out
events.text: Nancy Mace finished fifth in the Republican primary for governor.

events.title: The runoffs
events.text: On 23 June Honeycutt beat Mark Smith, 53.7 percent, and Lacore beat Mac Deford, 52.1.

events.title: Trump endorses
events.text: On 14 July President Trump endorsed Honeycutt.

events.title: Red to Blue
events.text: On 20 August the Democrats' campaign committee added Lacore to its Red to Blue programme.

events.title: First debate
events.text: On 7 October Honeycutt and Lacore debated on WCBD and WSAV.

events.title: Second debate
events.text: On 15 October Honeycutt and Lacore debated again, on WCSC Live 5.

events.title: Early voting
events.text: Early voting runs from 19 to 31 October, Monday to Saturday, 8:30 a.m. to 6 p.m.

events.title: Election Day
events.text: On 3 November polls are open from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m.

eras: New lines and an open seat
chartNote: Each state is coloured by the margin of the most recent presidential popular vote (Democratic minus Republican share of all votes; FEC certified results). It is a simplification: the 1st District is one of seven in South Carolina and elects its member of Congress in its own race; on today's lines it voted for Donald Trump by about 13 points in 2024 (The Downballot's calculation), against about 18 statewide, and it elected a Democrat in 2018. The presidential colour is a backdrop, not a forecast. Shares are of land area, not of people or votes. Boundaries are today's states (Natural Earth); the map is framed on South Carolina, so outer states are cut at the edge.
